Abstract:
<jats:p>The accelerating complexity of wireless hardware systems, driven by the proliferation of multistandard radios, multi-band front-ends, and highly integrated system-on-chip platforms, has made
manual RF test methodologies increasingly inadequate for the validation workloads of modern
hardware engineering laboratories. Test automation, the systematic use of scripting frameworks
and programmable instrument control interfaces to execute RF measurement sequences without
manual intervention, has emerged as a foundational engineering discipline that determines the
throughput, repeatability, and traceability of wireless hardware characterization workflows. This
paper presents a comprehensive review of test automation architectures, scripting frameworks,
and instrument control strategies applicable to wireless hardware engineering. The review
examines the evolution of automation approaches from early GPIB-based sequential scripting to
modern Python-based asynchronous measurement orchestration, covering standard
communication protocols including SCPI, LXI, and VISA, scripting environments including
Python, MATLAB, and LabVIEW, specialized RF test frameworks including Keysight PathWave
and National Instruments TestStand, and emerging approaches based on cloud-connected
measurement architectures and machine learning-assisted measurement optimization. The paper
synthesizes design principles for constructing automation frameworks that maximize measurement
throughput while maintaining calibration traceability, and identifies the key challenges of timing
synchronization, instrument state management, error recovery, and data provenance that
differentiate professionally engineered automation systems from ad hoc scripts. A structured
taxonomy of automation approaches is presented according to test complexity, measurement speed
requirement, and deployment context. The review concludes by identifying the most significant
open challenges in wireless hardware test automation, including automated calibration
verification, uncertainty-aware measurement pipelines, and the integration of AI-based anomaly
detection into production test workflows.</jats:p>

is making that information computable, with institutional digitization tending to focus more on imaging the specimens themselves than on efficiently capturing computable data about them. Label data are traditionally manually transcribed today with high cost and low throughput, rendering such a task constrained for many collection-holding institutions at current funding levels. We show how computer vision, optical character recognition, handwriting recognition, named entity recognition and language translation technologies can be implemented into canonical workflow component libraries with findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) characteristics. These libraries are being developed in a cloud-based workflow platform—the ‘Specimen Data Refinery’ (SDR)—founded on Galaxy workflow engine, Common Workflow Language, Research Object Crates (RO-Crate) and WorkflowHub technologies. Two kinds of FAIR Digital Objects (FDO) are created by packaging outputs of SDR workflows and workflow components as digital objects with metadata, a persistent identifier, and a specific type definition. The first kind of FDO are computable Digital Specimen (DS) objects that can be consumed/produced by workflows, and other applications. A single DS is the input data structure submitted to a workflow that is modified by each workflow component in turn to produce a refined DS at the end. The Specimen Data Refinery provides a library of such components that can be used individually, or in series. To cofunction, each library component describes the fields it requires from the DS and the fields it will in turn populate or enrich. The second kind of FDO, RO-Crates gather and archive the diverse set of digital and real-world resources, configurations, and actions (the provenance) contributing to a unit of research work, allowing that work to be faithfully recorded and reproduced. ## pqac-00000021

From text 'mutzenich2022situationawarenessin pages 190-193'.

C Mutzenich. Situation awareness in remote vehicle operators. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt indicates that remote supervision requires autonomous systems to enter a minimal risk condition (MRC), typically a safe stop, before an operator is asked to intervene. Because the operator may drop into an unfamiliar situation without prior monitoring, the interface must support rapid situation-awareness acquisition. Visual feedback quality, camera coverage, and information presentation format are critical; HMD-360 presentation reduced decision time compared with standard-broadband viewing, although responses still took approximately 2–12 seconds depending on the edge case and display format. Latency is a major safety concern: stale or delayed video can prevent the operator from recognizing hazards, while delayed control commands can affect turning, acceleration, and braking. A reported 3–4 second latency spike caused an operator to miss that the vehicle was approaching warehouse racks, creating crash risk without independent safety systems such as lidar. Supplementary camera feeds can help preserve awareness, but only if complete feeds are restored quickly and the operator can use them confidently. The excerpt also notes that loss of audio can further reduce available information in real operation. Remote supervision therefore imposes greater situational-awareness demands than in-situ driving, and conventional driving SA measures may be inappropriate. It does not provide detailed bandwidth specifications, video-resolution requirements, out-of-the-loop performance measurements, or a specific remote emergency-stop design beyond the MRC concept.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'mutzenich2022situationawarenessin pages 35-36'.

C Mutzenich. Situation awareness in remote vehicle operators. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt identifies several requirements for remote supervision of autonomous vehicles. Communication must provide very low and, importantly, consistent latency: delays above approximately 50 ms make the displayed imagery outdated for useful interaction, while 5G may reduce latency to below 10 ms. LabRobFail-Bench evaluates VLMs on six dimensions: task understanding (Q1), binary failure detection (Q2), temporal localization (Q3), severity assessment (Q4), failure classification (Q5), and correction strategy (Q6). On the reported seen-environment test, LabRobFail-VLM substantially outperforms the listed general-purpose baselines. Its accuracies are 94.45% for task understanding, 90.83% for failure detection, 77.21% for temporal localization, 83.18% for severity assessment, and 73.21% for failure classification. By comparison, baseline detection accuracy ranges from 47.04% to 59.50%, while localization is especially weak, ranging from 5.59% to 15.88%. LabRobFail-VLM also achieves much higher correction scores (BLEU-1 through BLEU-4: 0.7629, 0.7569, 0.7452, and 0.7362; ROUGE-L: 0.7542). These results indicate strong benchmark performance, particularly for detecting failures, but they do not by themselves establish that the system is safe enough for autonomous safety-critical gating. Detection remains imperfect at 90.83%, localization and failure classification are lower, and the benchmark concerns chemical hazards capable of catastrophic damage or injury. Additional validation, uncertainty handling, fail-safe design, and near-zero-false-negative testing would be needed before relying on a VLM as the sole gate.

Abstract:
While there is no rigorous framework to develop nanosatellites flight software, this manuscript aimed to explore and establish processes to design a reliable and reusable flight software architecture for cost-efficient student Cubesat missions such as Masat-1. Masat-1 is a 1Unit CubeSat, developed using a systems engineering approach, off-the-shelf components and open-source software tools. It was our aim to use it as a test-bed platform and as an initial reference for Cubesat flight software development in Morocco. The command and data handling system chosen for Masat-1 is a system-on-module-embedded computer running freeRTOS. A real-time operating system was used in order to simplify the real-time onboard management. To ensure software design reliability, modularity, reusability and extensibility, our solution follows a layered service oriented architectural pattern, and it is based on a finite state machine in the application layer to execute the mission functionalities in a deterministic manner. Moreover, a client-server model was elected to ensure the inter-process communication and resources access while using uniform APIs to enhance cross-platform data exchange. A hierarchical fault tolerance architecture was also implemented after a systematic assessment of the Masat-1 mission risks using reliability block diagrams (RBDs) and functional failure mode, effect and criticality analysis (FMECA).

Abstract:
Traditional anomaly detection techniques onboard satellites are based on reliable, yet limited, thresholding mechanisms which are designed to monitor univariate signals and trigger recovery actions according to specific European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) standards. However, Artificial Intelligence-based Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR) solutions have recently raised with the prospect to overcome the limitations of these standard methods, expanding the range of detectable failures and improving response times. The paper presents the initial outcomes of a project, currently ongoing under the supervision of the European Space Agency, having the main objective to specify and design a Fault Detection Isolation and Recovery (FDIR) system by making use of relevant RAMS (Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, Safety) analyses for missions in non-deterministic environment with limited resources. <jats:p>The increasing complexity of spacecraft On-Board Software (OBSW) necessitates advanced development and testing methodologies to ensure reliability and robustness. This paper presents a digital twin approach for the development and testing of embedded spacecraft software. The proposed electronic digital twin enables high-fidelity hardware and software simulations of spacecraft subsystems, facilitating a comprehensive validation framework. Through real-time execution, the digital twin supports dynamical simulations with possibility of failure injections, enabling the observation of software behavior under various nominal or fault conditions. This capability allows for thorough debugging and verification of critical software components, including Finite State Machines (FSM), Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) algorithms, and platform and mode management logic. By providing an interactive and iterative environment for software validation in nominal and contingency scenarios, the digital twin reduces the need for extensive Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing, accelerating the software development life-cycle while improving reliability. The paper discusses the architecture and implementation of the digital twin, along with case studies based on a modular OBSW architecture, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying and resolving software anomalies. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable solution for spacecraft software development, enhancing mission safety and performance.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Designing on-board computers (OBC) for future space missions is determined by the trade-off between reliability and performance. Space applications with higher computational demands are not supported by currently available, state-of-the-art, space-qualified computing hardware, since their requirements exceed the capabilities of these components. Such space applications include Earth observation with high-resolution cameras, on-orbit real-time servicing, as well as autonomous spacecraft and rover missions on distant celestial bodies. An alternative to state-of-the-art space-qualified computing hardware is the use of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) components for the OBC. Not only are these components cheap and widely available, but they also achieve high performance. Unfortunately, they are also significantly more vulnerable to errors induced by radiation than space-qualified components. The ScOSA (Scalable On-board Computing for Space Avionics) Flight Experiment project aims to develop an OBC architecture which avoids this trade-off by combining space-qualified radiation-hardened components (the reliable computing nodes, RCNs) together with COTS components (the high performance nodes, HPNs) into a single distributed system. To abstract this heterogeneous architecture for the application developers, we are developing a middleware for the aforementioned OBC architecture. Besides providing an monolithic abstraction of the distributed system, the middleware shall also enhance the architecture by providing additional reliability and fault tolerance. In this paper, we present the individual components comprising the middleware, alongside the features the middleware offers. Since the ScOSA Flight Experiment project is a successor of the OBC-NG and the ScOSA projects, its middleware is also a further development of the existing middleware. Therefore, we will present and discuss our contributions and plans for enhancement of the middleware in the course of the current project. Finally, we will present first results for the scalability of the middleware, which we obtained by conducting software-in-the-loop experiments of different sized scenarios.

Abstract:
The standardization of the physical aspects of nanosatellites (also known as CubeSats) and their wide adoption in academia and industry has made the mass production and availability of off-the-shelf components possible. While this has led to a significant reduction in satellite development time, the fact remains that a considerable amount of mission development time and effort continues to be spent on flight software development. The CubeSat’s agile development environment makes it challenging to utilize the advantages of existing software frameworks. Such an adoption is not straightforward due to the added complexity characterized by a steep learning curve. A well-designed flight software architecture mitigates possible sources of failure and increases mission success rate while maintaining moderate complexity. This paper presents a novel approach to a flight software framework developed specifically for nanosatellites. The software framework is characterized by simplicity, reliability, modularity, portability, and real-time capability. The main features of the proposed framework include providing a standardized and explicit skeleton for each module to simplify their construction, offering standardized interfaces for all modules to simplify communication, and providing a collection of ready-to-use common services open for further enhancement by CubeSat software developers. The framework efficiency was demonstrated through a software developed for the MeznSat mission that was successfully launched into Low Earth Orbit in September 2020. The proposed software framework proved to simplify software development for the application developer while significantly enhancing software modularity.

Abstract:
The material acceleration platform, empowered by robotics and artificial intelligence, is a transformative approach for expediting material discovery processes across diverse domains. However, the development of an operating system for material acceleration platform faces challenges in simultaneously managing diverse experiments from multiple users. Specifically, when it is utilized by multiple users, the overlapping challenges of experimental modules or devices can lead to inefficiencies in both resource utilization and safety hazards. To overcome these challenges, we present an operation control system for material acceleration platform, namely, OCTOPUS, which is an acronym for operation control system for task optimization and job parallelization via a user-optimal scheduler. OCTOPUS streamlines experiment scheduling and optimizes resource utilization through integrating its interface node, master node and module nodes. Leveraging process modularization and a network protocol, OCTOPUS ensures the homogeneity, scalability, safety and versatility of the platform. In addition, OCTOPUS embodies a user-optimal scheduler. Job parallelization and task optimization techniques mitigate delays and safety hazards within realistic operational environments, while the closed-packing schedule algorithm efficiently executes multiple jobs with minimal resource waste. Copilot of OCTOPUS is developed to promote the reusability of OCTOPUS for potential users with their own sets of lab resources, which substantially simplifies the process of code generation and customization through GPT recommendations and client feedback. This work offers a solution to the challenges encountered within the platform accessed by multiple users, and thereby will facilitate its widespread adoption in material development processes.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Scientific discovery is fundamentally a problem-solving process involving distributed intelligence. Human intuition, computational reasoning, and experimental execution are distributed across people, instruments, and software systems, limiting the speed and scale of discovery. Although automation, high-throughput experimentation, foundation models, and cloud infrastructure have accelerated individual stages of the scientific workflow, they have not unified the discovery process. We hypothesize that the next generation of laboratories will be agentic: environments in which scientists, AI systems, and robotic platforms operate as collaborative discovery partners, with humans contributing the parts of discovery that remain hardest to make explicit: asking the right questions and holding provisional mechanistic models of how a system works. The key missing layer is an agentic harnessing layer that continuously integrates hypothesis, literature-derived evidence, experimental data, uncertainty, and experimental state into a shared “laboratory world model”—a dynamic representation of the scientific system and its evolving context. By maintaining and updating this lab world model, the agentic harnessing layer enables coordinated decision-making, adaptive planning, and increasingly autonomous scientific workflows across humans and machines. A central challenge is that much of the scientific research process remains inaccessible to machines, including tacit knowledge, human observations, adaptive decision-making, and evolving experimental context. Advances in multimodal AI and immersive interfaces may help bridge this gap, allowing humans, agents, and robotic systems to collaborate seamlessly in scientific discovery rather than simply automating isolated tasks. Agentic laboratories could provide a new architecture for science, integrating human, artificial, and physical intelligence into a unified discovery system.</jats:p>

For safety and operational resilience, OCTOPUS includes network-level emergency stopping, heartbeat/shutdown mechanisms using UDP broadcast, and messenger-based alerts and monitoring. Its broader orchestration distinction is TCP/IP-based process modularization, allowing heterogeneous devices and selectively assembled modules, rather than a platform restricted to one application. Include rows for: ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025), ISO/TS 15066, ISO 13849-1, IEC 62061, IEC 61508, ANSI/RIA R15.06, OSHA General Duty Clause (29 CFR 1910.212), NFPA 484, ISO 12100. Include rows for: Aluminium (10 \u03bcm) with Kst 14.40 MPa\u00b7m/s = ~144 bar\u00b7m/s and Pmax 0.64 MPa from Chen et al. 2022; Aluminium (20 \u03bcm) with Kst 4.33 MPa\u00b7m/s = ~43 bar\u00b7m/s and Pmax 0.52 MPa; Silicon (~typical) with Kst ~120 bar\u00b7m/s from Reding et al. 2019; AlSi10Mg (note this is an alloy, test data more limited). Include MIE values noting Al is typically 10-50 mJ for fine powder (extrapolation flag). Note that all values are particle-size dependent and these are specific test conditions. Dust class: St1 (<200), St2 (200-300), St3 (>300). Note that fine Al at optimum concentration can reach St3."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Standard | Scope | Key Requirements for This SDL | Legally Binding in US University? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 | Safety of industrial robots and integrated robot applications; Part 1 addresses robot manufacturers, Part 2 integrators and robot cells. | Perform cell-level risk assessment; define safeguarded, restricted, operational, and collaborative spaces; provide validated protective stops, emergency stops, mode control, access protection, restart prevention, and integration/validation documentation. The complete arm–tool–workpiece–furnace cell must be assessed—not merely the PiPER arm. Collaborative operation does not remove guarding requirements where hot, sharp, reactive, or crushing hazards cannot be acceptably limited. (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **Usually not directly statutory.** A voluntary consensus standard, but it may become the recognized benchmark through contracts, university EHS policy, insurer conditions, an adopted code, or OSHA evidence of feasible hazard control. | The 2025 revision should be checked against the institution’s adopted ANSI/RIA edition. It does not grant blanket permission for unattended operation; suitability follows from the application risk assessment and validated safety functions. Published SDL literature located here does not demonstrate third-party ISO 10218 certification. (pqac-00000070, pqac-00000072) |
| ISO/TS 15066:2016 | Supplemental guidance for collaborative industrial robot applications. | Select and validate one or more collaborative methods: safety-rated monitored stop, hand guiding, speed-and-separation monitoring, or power-and-force limiting. Assess the end effector, payload, fixtures, trapping geometry, transient contact, and quasi-static contact—not just nominal arm force. (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **No, unless incorporated** into policy, contract, approval conditions, or a legally enforceable duty. | It addresses human–robot collaboration, not furnace, combustible-dust, or reactive-material safety. If nobody is present, “collaborative” capability is largely irrelevant; hazardous process and unexpected-entry risks still require safeguarding. |
| ISO 13849-1:2023 | Design of safety-related parts of machinery control systems using Performance Levels, PL a–e. | Derive the required PL for each safety function from risk; design suitable architecture/category, component reliability, diagnostic coverage, common-cause-failure resistance, and systematic controls. Validate separately under ISO 13849-2. Safety functions may include guard-door stopping, restart inhibit, emergency stop, furnace-door permissives, and exhaust/grounding interlocks. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) | **Not independently statutory**, but commonly used to substantiate that safety controls meet the recognized state of practice. | PL is assigned **per safety function**, not to the laboratory as a whole. A PL e-capable relay cannot make an uncertified robot reaction path PL e; end-to-end claims require evidence for sensing, logic, output, and final stopping elements. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| IEC 62061:2021 | Functional safety of safety-related control systems for machinery using SIL 1–3 and SIL claim limits. | Determine required SIL for each safety-related control function; allocate and verify integrity across sensors, logic, communication, and actuators; control random hardware and systematic failures; validate the integrated function. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) | **Not independently statutory** in the United States; an alternative machinery-functional-safety route that EHS, integrators, or insurers may accept. | Do not casually translate PL to SIL or claim SIL 3 because individual components support it. The complete safety function and its interfaces must satisfy the claimed integrity. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003) |
| IEC 61508 series | Generic lifecycle standard for electrical/electronic/programmable-electronic functional safety systems. | Apply a safety lifecycle where machinery-specific standards do not adequately cover a function: hazard analysis, safety requirements allocation, independence, systematic-capability controls, verification, validation, configuration management, proof testing, and change control. | **Normally not directly binding** on a university SDL. It may be invoked contractually or used as the parent framework for a separately engineered safety-instrumented function. | ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061 is ordinarily more directly applicable to machinery. IEC 61508 is not a certification shortcut for Raspberry Pis, MQTT, ordinary PLCs, cameras, or cloud services. (pqac-00000074) |

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table titled "90-Day Safety-First Implementation Timeline" with columns: Phase, Days, Activity, Category (Legal Requirement / Best Practice / Prudent but Optional), Prerequisite, and Deliverable. Include:

Phase 0 (Days 1-14): Risk assessment and documentation - ISO 12100 risk assessment of the full cell (legally required for OSHA compliance), STPA of the control structure, dust hazard analysis per NFPA 484/660, EHS pre-submission meeting, emergency stop chain design, grounding/bonding survey of powder handling area. All legal requirement or best practice.

Phase 1 (Days 15-35): Physical safety infrastructure - Install hardwired e-stop chain with safety relay (legal requirement), install grounding/bonding on all powder-handling equipment (legal requirement), install Class D fire extinguisher and train users (legal requirement), install fume hood exhaust verification interlock, install polycarbonate enclosure around PiPER with interlocked door, configure furnace door interlock (arm power disabled while door open), submit documentation package to institutional EHS.

Phase 2 (Days 36-60): Software safety layer and attended commissioning - Implement watchdog/heartbeat on PiPER controller, implement workspace envelope limits in software, deploy MQTT-based state machine with safe-state transitions, commission sandbox primitives from Q3 under attended observation, validate e-stop chain end-to-end, implement remote monitoring (cameras, alerting), begin logging and provenance system.

Phase 3 (Days 61-90): Supervised unattended trials - First unattended overnight run: arm-only pick-and-place with no powder, no furnace, with remote monitoring and auto-halt on anomaly. Progressive: add balance-loop powder dispensing under attended then remote supervision. Build run-hours and incident log for progressive autonomy case. First experiment without a person in the room: inert powder (e.g., alumina) dispensing and weighing loop. NOT reactive metal powder unattended in 90 days.

Make clear that reactive metal powder handling unattended is NOT achievable in 90 days and requires demonstrated incident-free hours and validated dust controls first."}

{"answer": "# Q4: Unattended Operation, Safety, and the Control Plane for a Cloud-Operated SDL

## 1. Standards, Regulations, and What Actually Binds a University Lab

### 1.1 The Standards Landscape

The relevant standards form a hierarchy. **ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025 revision)** addresses industrial robot safety at the manufacturer and integrator level, requiring a cell-level risk assessment that covers safeguarded, restricted, operational, and collaborative spaces, validated protective stops, emergency stops, and integration documentation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). **ISO/TS 15066** supplements ISO 10218 with guidance on the four collaborative operation modes: safety-rated monitored stop (SRMS), hand guiding, speed-and-separation monitoring (SSM), and power-and-force limiting (PFL), with body-region-specific transient and quasi-static contact force and pressure limits (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Example collaborative cobot limits cited are 0.23 m/s speed, 149 N force, and 79 W dynamic power (pqac-00000051).

**ISO 13849-1** provides the Performance Level (PL a–e) framework for safety-related parts of control systems, requiring each safety function to be designed to an architecture category with appropriate component reliability, diagnostic coverage, and common-cause failure resistance. **IEC 62061** provides a parallel SIL claim limit (SILCL) assessment. In the humanoid robot feasibility study, the external detection and evaluation subsystems each achieved PL e / SILCL 3, but the robot-side reaction chain remained uncertifiable because the PiPER—like any uncertified low-cost arm—lacks a characterized probability of dangerous failure per hour (PFHD) for its stopping behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). **IEC 61508** is the parent generic functional safety lifecycle standard; it is not normally applied directly to machinery but may be invoked where ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061 do not adequately cover a function (pqac-00000074).

A critical point: PL and SIL are assigned **per safety function**, not to the laboratory as a whole. A PL e-rated safety relay cannot retroactively make an uncertified robot reaction path PL e; the entire chain from sensor through logic to final element must satisfy the claimed integrity (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

The following table summarizes which standards bind a US university laboratory:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 1.2 The US Regulatory and Institutional Reality

In the United States, the ISO standards are voluntary consensus standards. They become effectively binding through several mechanisms: (a) OSHA's General Duty Clause (OSH Act §5(a)(1)) requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized serious hazards, and consensus standards serve as evidence of recognized practice; (b) **ANSI/RIA R15.06** is the US national robot safety consensus standard, historically harmonized with ISO 10218 (pqac-00000070); (c) university EHS committees and institutional review processes typically require documented risk assessments and may impose specific standards as conditions of approval; and (d) insurers may require compliance with specific standards as conditions of coverage.

**What published SDLs have actually done:** No published self-driving laboratory located in this review has documented formal third-party ISO 10218 certification or a completed ISO 13849-1 PL validation for its robot safety functions (pqac-00000072, pqac-00000073). The most comprehensive published safety architecture is **Safe-SDL**, which proposes a defense-in-depth framework with Operational Design Domains (ODDs), Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), and a CRUTD transactional safety protocol, but explicitly frames these as architectural proposals rather than certified implementations (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). This is a significant gap in the field: the SDL community has published extensively on workflow orchestration and optimization but very little on formal safety engineering.

### 1.3 Risk Assessment Methodology

For an SDL that combines software-controlled robots, furnaces, reactive powders, and remote supervision, **STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis)** is the most appropriate primary hazard analysis method. STPA models the system as a hierarchical control structure and examines unsafe control actions (UCAs) and causal scenarios across controllers, software, humans, and the environment (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Unlike FMEA, which focuses on individual component failures, STPA can address system-level interactions, feedback loops, software errors, and hazards that arise without any component failing—precisely the kind of scenario where an autonomous retry loop or a stale MQTT message causes harm (pqac-00000016). HAZOP is valuable for the furnace and powder-handling process nodes but requires adaptation for software-intensive systems (pqac-00000016). The recommended approach is: **ISO 12100** as the overall risk assessment framework, supplemented by **STPA** for the control structure, **HAZOP** for the furnace/powder process, and **FMEA/FMECA** for hardware component faults.

## 2. Specific Hazards, Quantified

### 2.1 Reactive Metal Powders

The dust explosion parameters for the powders in this system are summarized below:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For 10 μm aluminium powder, the maximum explosion pressure was 0.64 MPa and the deflagration index (Kst) was approximately 144 bar·m/s, measured at 200 g/m³ in a 20 L sphere (pqac-00000012). For 20 μm aluminium, Kst dropped to approximately 43 bar·m/s (pqac-00000012). Silicon dust has a reported Kst of approximately 120 bar·m/s at optimum concentration (pqac-00000013). These values are strongly particle-size dependent and must be obtained through lot-specific testing rather than handbook lookup (pqac-00000013). AlSi10Mg alloy-specific data were not found in the reviewed literature and must be tested independently.

**Static from a printed enclosure or plastic funnel is a real ignition source.** The MIE of fine aluminium powder is typically in the range of 10–50 mJ (extrapolation flagged—obtain lot-specific data), which is well within the energy range of electrostatic discharges from insulating plastic surfaces. FDM-printed enclosures (PLA, PETG, ABS) are insulators that can accumulate static charge during powder transfer. A powder-contact funnel or chute printed on a Bambu Lab printer would be an ungrounded insulating surface capable of generating brush discharges with energy sufficient to ignite fine aluminium dust. All conductive powder-handling equipment must be bonded and grounded with verified continuity. Non-conductive components must be replaced with static-dissipative or conductive alternatives, or eliminated from the powder-contact path.

**Enclosure and exhaust design:** The fume hood provides containment and local exhaust ventilation, but the exhaust system must be designed for combustible metal dust. Aluminium dust must not be routed into a general-purpose dust collector or a wet scrubber where water contact with fine aluminium could generate hydrogen. A dedicated, NFPA 484/660-compliant collection system with spark-resistant ductwork and appropriate isolation is required where adopted codes apply.

**Class D fire suppression:** Burning aluminium reacts violently with water (steam explosion risk and hydrogen generation) and with CO₂ (aluminium reduces CO₂ to carbon and aluminium oxide, sustaining combustion). Standard ABC extinguishers, water sprinklers, and CO₂ systems are all contraindicated. A Class D extinguishing agent (e.g., Met-L-X, sodium chloride-based, or dry sand) must be provided, and all on-site personnel must be trained to recognize that applying water to a metal fire will make it catastrophically worse.

### 2.2 Furnace Hazards

The critical furnace scenario is: the arm faults mid-insert with the furnace door open. If the safety system unconditionally removes arm power, the arm may drop a hot crucible, creating a spill of hot material and potentially a powder ignition event. The safe-state design must account for this: a mid-insert fault should trigger a controlled arm retraction or a hold-in-place before power removal, with the furnace door closing only after the arm is confirmed clear of the aperture. This requires a cause-and-effect matrix that addresses the arm, furnace, and their interaction states. Safe-SDL identifies thermal runaway and exothermic reactions as domain-specific hazards requiring real-time monitoring, forward prediction against a safe set, and automated shutdown (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008).

### 2.3 The Arm Itself

The AgileX PiPER is a 6-DOF arm with 1.5 kg payload and 626 mm reach, costing approximately $3k. At this price point, it almost certainly does not have certified safety-rated monitored stop, certified safe torque off, or validated stopping-time characterization with a published PFHD. This means the arm **cannot independently claim any Performance Level under ISO 13849-1** for its stopping behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). An external safety relay, hardwired e-stop chain, and guard interlocking are not merely advisable—they are the only mechanism by which a defensible safety function can be constructed. The e-stop chain must use positive-opening contacts, dual-channel monitoring, manual reset with restart inhibit, and must not pass through MQTT, Tailscale, a Raspberry Pi, or any ordinary computing element.

At 1.5 kg payload and modest speed, the pinch and crush hazard is moderate but not negligible. A 1.5 kg payload at 1 m/s generates approximately 0.75 J of kinetic energy; the hazard is dominated by trapping geometry (e.g., crushing a finger between a crucible and a fixture) rather than free-space impact. The polycarbonate enclosure with interlocked access door is the primary mitigation for unexpected entry.

## 3. Fault Detection, Containment, and Safe-State Design

### 3.1 Spacecraft FDIR as the Transferable Model

The spacecraft Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) architecture provides the most directly transferable guard architecture for an SDL. In the Masat-1 CubeSat, FDIR is organized hierarchically: housekeeping collectors and safety functions detect component-level problems; a safety monitor correlates events with actions; and the flight planner makes the highest-level FDIR decisions (pqac-00000035). Recovery is attempted through command retries, parameter defaulting, watchdog-triggered resets, and receiver reinitialization. External EPS watchdogs periodically ping the onboard computer; after five failed pings they reset it. For unresolvable faults, the system transitions to a fail-safe mode: non-vital units are powered down and the spacecraft adopts a thermally and energetically safe configuration until ground contact (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038).

For an SDL, this translates to:
- **Level 0 (device):** Current/torque limits, encoder watchdogs, temperature monitors on each device.
- **Level 1 (subsystem):** Workspace envelope violation, balance disagreement, camera loss, stale heartbeat → local stop and retry (bounded).
- **Level 2 (orchestrator):** Mass-balance audit failure, protocol-sequence violation, consumed/remaining inventory mismatch → HOLD state and alert.
- **Level 3 (supervisor):** Escalation to human, system-wide safe state, furnace shutdown, ventilation assurance.

### 3.2 VLM Supervision: Useful but Not Safety-Critical

The LabRobFail benchmark evaluated vision-language models for robotic failure detection in chemical SDLs. The specialized LabRobFail-VLM achieves 90.83% failure-detection accuracy on seen environments, 77.21% temporal localization, and 83.18% severity assessment (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030). However, under distribution shift (unseen objects and scenes), detection accuracy drops to 71.02%, and temporal localization falls to 41.41% (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). These results are explicitly insufficient for safety-critical gating: a 29% miss rate on unseen conditions is far below the >99% reliability needed for a safety interlock (pqac-00000031). A VLM supervisor is appropriately used as a **supplementary anomaly-detection channel** that can trigger a HOLD state and page a human, but it must not be the sole gate on a hazardous action.

### 3.3 Safe-SDL's CRUTD Protocol

Safe-SDL proposes a transactional safety protocol: Create a request → Read/lock resources and capture state → simulate the transition → Test constraints → execute under monitoring → confirm the achieved state → abort/rollback on failure (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000061). This directly addresses the Q1 provenance failure where insert time was conflated with measurement time: the protocol separates requested, validated, executed, and confirmed states with distinct timestamps.

### 3.4 Recovery vs. Halt: The Autonomous Retry Problem

The critical design question is: when should the system retry, and when should it halt and page a human? The spacecraft pattern is clear: bounded local recovery at the lowest level, with escalation on failure (pqac-00000037). The SDL equivalent is:
- **Retry:** A balance reading that disagrees by <1% on first attempt → re-weigh once. A gripper position error within repeatability → re-approach once.
- **Halt:** A balance disagreement >5%, a dropped object, a current spike, an unrecognized object in the workspace, any thermal anomaly, any loss of communication with safety-critical devices, or **any second consecutive failure of the same type**.

The autonomous retry loop that converts a recoverable fault into a catastrophic one is the most dangerous failure mode. The design rule is: **finite retry budget (typically 1–2), monotonically decreasing scope with each retry, automatic escalation to HOLD after budget exhaustion, and human-cleared recovery from HOLD** (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000036).

## 3b. Remote Supervision

### Latency, Bandwidth, and Video Quality

Remote vehicle operation studies indicate that communication latency above approximately 50 ms makes displayed imagery outdated for useful interaction; 5G networks may reduce latency below 10 ms (pqac-00000022). Streaming video from four HD cameras requires at least 50 Mbit/s (pqac-00000022). A latency spike of 3–4 seconds caused a remote operator to miss that a vehicle was approaching warehouse racks, creating crash risk (pqac-00000021). For an SDL, this means the Tailscale VPN must provide consistent sub-100 ms round-trip latency, and the system must automatically transition to HOLD if video latency exceeds a defined threshold.

### The Out-of-the-Loop Problem

When a remote human is only summoned on exception, recovery time depends critically on the specificity of the alert. A specified failure (e.g., "balance timeout on station 3") took approximately 29 seconds to understand, whereas an unspecified problem took approximately 162 seconds (pqac-00000022). This is a factor of 5.6×, which has direct implications for alarm design: every alert must include the failure type, affected station, current system state, available actions, and recommended response. HMD-360 presentation produced faster decisions than screen-based viewing—approximately 80% of screen-based decision time and more than twice as many correct responses (pqac-00000025).

### Remote E-Stop Design

When the responsible human is 1,000 km away and the only people in the room are undergraduates who did not start the experiment, the e-stop system must satisfy two independent requirements: (a) a **physical e-stop button** accessible to anyone in the room, clearly labeled, requiring no knowledge of the experiment, connected to the hardwired safety chain, and (b) a **remote stop command** that is software-initiated but terminates in a hardwired safety relay or contactor, not merely an MQTT message. The remote stop must be tested end-to-end, and the system must enter a safe state automatically on loss of the remote supervision link (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). Maritime autonomous system requirements specify that communication links must be treated as safety-control channels, with link quality monitored and tied to operational-state thresholds (pqac-00000024).

## 4. The Control Plane

### 4.1 Critical Evaluation of EOS vs. Existing Infrastructure

The group's existing stack is **MQTT (HiveMQ) + MongoDB Atlas + Hugging Face Spaces + GitHub Actions**, with Tailscale networking and an Opentrons HTTP API. Q3 recommended EOS. The migration cost of adopting EOS or any monolithic SDL orchestrator would be substantial: it would require replacing or wrapping the existing MQTT device bus, re-implementing the Opentrons integration, migrating the MongoDB data model, and retraining students on a new framework—all for uncertain gain given the group's already-functioning device communication layer.

**The defensible architecture keeps MQTT as the device bus and adds an orchestrator above it.** This is precisely the pattern used by OCTOPUS, which implements a hierarchical client/interface-node/master-node/module-node architecture with TCP/IP-based process modularization, supporting concurrent multi-user jobs from heterogeneous devices (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000067). OCTOPUS's user-optimal scheduler reduced example total job times from 10 to 5.5–6.5 hours compared to first-come-first-served serialization (pqac-00000062).

**What MQTT alone lacks and what must be added above it:**
- **Multi-user queuing and fair scheduling:** MQTT is a pub/sub bus, not a scheduler. An orchestrator must maintain job queues, unique job IDs, resource locks, and a scheduling policy (pqac-00000067).
- **Authentication and authorization:** HiveMQ supports ACLs, but experiment-level authorization (who may run what protocol with what materials) requires an application-layer gate.
- **Crash recovery and idempotency:** MQTT QoS 2 provides at-most-once or exactly-once message delivery, but protocol-level crash recovery requires durable state: each command must have an idempotency key, and the orchestrator must be able to resume from a known good state after restart.
- **Observability:** MongoDB provides storage but not real-time dashboards. Add structured event streams with timestamps, state assertions, and health metrics.

### 4.2 Data Provenance and Persistent Identifiers

**RO-Crate** packages research objects—data, workflows, software, metadata, and provenance—into self-describing JSON-LD containers using Schema.org vocabulary (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000060). **PROV-O** provides the W3C ontology for representing provenance: entities, activities, and agents with generation, usage, derivation, and attribution relationships (pqac-00000055). Together, they can package an SDL campaign: the requested protocol, the authorized execution plan, the sensor-observed physical events, the resulting data, and the complete chain of custody.

The Q1 failure—conflating insert time with measurement time—is precisely the provenance failure that RO-Crate + PROV-O is designed to prevent. A prospective instrument trace should record each experimental event with its control source (human, script, optimizer, agent), distinguishing the requested action from the executed action from the observed outcome (pqac-00000059). The CRUTD protocol from Safe-SDL provides the operational model: the requested command, the pre-operation state snapshot, the simulation/validation result, the execution event, the post-execution sensor confirmation, and any abort/rollback events should all be recorded as distinct provenance entities with separate timestamps (pqac-00000061).

For DOI minting: package completed campaigns as Workflow-Run RO-Crates, deposit to Zenodo, and mint DOIs. This provides immutable, citable records of what physically happened.

## 5. Human Factors and the Undergraduate Reality

### 5.1 Training and Error Rates

The SDL literature is qualitatively consistent: human technicians remain essential for loading plates, opening packages, replacing consumables, replenishing reagents, removing waste, calibrating equipment, and resolving faults (pqac-00000043). Laboratory automation is generally fixed and highly structured, requiring carefully specified layouts; even small equipment or consumable changes can require substantial reprogramming (pqac-00000043). Virtual reality training has been shown to reduce operator errors, but may increase stress for complex tasks due to the greater information load (from the Brunzini et al. 2024 training methodology study).

### 5.2 Human Time Costs in SDLs

No published SDL located in this review provides quantitative utilization rates (percentage of wall-clock time spent running vs. idle) or calibrated human-time savings. The qualitative evidence is consistent: autonomous Bayesian optimization campaigns have reached optima in under 30 hours, and batched reaction optimization achieved 192 reactions in four days—approximately 4× the throughput of sequential human operation (pqac-00000046). However, these throughput gains are interleaved with human effort for electrode cleaning, vial loading, chemical preparation, purification troubleshooting, and consumable replacement (pqac-00000045). Dispensing solids below approximately 20 mg and handling heterogeneous mixtures remain difficult to automate (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048).

### 5.3 Design Choices That Improve Utilization

The most impactful design choices are: (a) **magazine/rack capacity** sized so that consumable exhaustion does not interrupt overnight runs; (b) **scheduled human touchpoints** (e.g., daily morning restocking) rather than on-demand interruptions; (c) **batching** to consolidate related experiments into continuous runs; (d) **finite consumable accounting** so the system knows when to stop before running out; and (e) **progressive autonomy** starting with the simplest, most constrained operations and expanding only after demonstrated reliability (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

**Flagged extrapolation:** The precise throughput fraction lost to restocking and low-utilization windows is not well-characterized in the published literature. This is an open measurement gap that this group could contribute to by instrumenting their own system.

## 6. The First 90 Days

The following phased timeline places risk assessment and physical safeguards before software commissioning and narrowly bounded unattended trials:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### Key Constraints

**The first experiment that can honestly run without a person in the room** is an inert-powder (alumina) dispensing-and-weighing loop, with no furnace, no reactive metals, restricted room access, remote monitoring, hardwired safeguards, finite consumable budget, and automatic halt on anomaly. This is achievable within 90 days if the safety infrastructure is in place.

**Reactive metal powder handling unattended is not a defensible 90-day milestone.** It requires lot-specific explosibility testing, validated dust-handling controls, approved exhaust/collection design, demonstrated static-control measures, incident-free attended and remotely supervised operating hours, and institutional/fire-authority approval. Treating a fume hood, a printed enclosure, a camera feed, or a remote operator as explosion protection is not defensible.

### Minimum Documentation Package for EHS Review

The minimum defensible package includes: (1) scope and system description; (2) ISO 12100 risk assessment register; (3) STPA control structure analysis; (4) dust hazard analysis per NFPA 484/660; (5) SDS inventory and quantity limits; (6) cell layout with safety distances; (7) safety circuit schematics with component ratings; (8) ventilation basis of design; (9) fire-response plan with Class D agent selection; (10) SOPs for attended and unattended operation; (11) training plan and competency records; (12) commissioning and validation protocol; (13) remote-supervision concept of operations; and (14) management-of-change procedure.

### What Is Legally Required vs. Best Practice vs. Prudent

- **Legally required** (where applicable): Risk assessment documenting recognized hazards and feasible controls (OSHA General Duty Clause); machine guarding (29 CFR 1910.212); combustible-metal fire prevention per adopted fire code; emergency-stop accessible to room occupants; training for all personnel.
- **Best practice:** ISO 12100 risk assessment framework; STPA for the control structure; ISO 13849-1 PL derivation for safety functions; Safe-SDL CRUTD protocol; RO-Crate provenance; progressive autonomy with regression after incidents.
- **Prudent but optional:** VLM anomaly detection as supplementary channel; immersive (HMD-360) remote supervision interface; formal verification of safety-kernel software; digital-twin pre-validation of each experiment.

### What Is Unknown

Several questions remain genuinely open: (1) no published SDL has reported a formal safety-validation protocol or third-party certification for its robot safety functions; (2) no quantitative SDL utilization data exist in the reviewed literature; (3) the AgileX PiPER's stopping-time characterization, PFHD, and diagnostic coverage are not publicly documented; (4) AlSi10Mg alloy-specific dust explosion parameters are not available in the reviewed literature; and (5) the long-term reliability of VLM-based anomaly detection under distribution shift in production SDL environments is an open research question (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032)."}

{"answer": "# Q4: Unattended Operation, Safety, and the Control Plane for a Cloud-Operated SDL

## 1. Standards, Regulations, and What Actually Binds a University Lab

### 1.1 The Standards Landscape

The relevant standards form a hierarchy. **ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025 revision)** addresses industrial robot safety at the manufacturer and integrator level, requiring a cell-level risk assessment that covers safeguarded, restricted, operational, and collaborative spaces, validated protective stops, emergency stops, and integration documentation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). **ISO/TS 15066** supplements ISO 10218 with guidance on the four collaborative operation modes: safety-rated monitored stop (SRMS), hand guiding, speed-and-separation monitoring (SSM), and power-and-force limiting (PFL), with body-region-specific transient and quasi-static contact force and pressure limits (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Example collaborative cobot limits cited are 0.23 m/s speed, 149 N force, and 79 W dynamic power (pqac-00000051).

**ISO 13849-1** provides the Performance Level (PL a–e) framework for safety-related parts of control systems, requiring each safety function to be designed to an architecture category with appropriate component reliability, diagnostic coverage, and common-cause failure resistance. **IEC 62061** provides a parallel SIL claim limit (SILCL) assessment. In the humanoid robot feasibility study, the external detection and evaluation subsystems each achieved PL e / SILCL 3, but the robot-side reaction chain remained uncertifiable because the PiPER—like any uncertified low-cost arm—lacks a characterized probability of dangerous failure per hour (PFHD) for its stopping behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). **IEC 61508** is the parent generic functional safety lifecycle standard; it is not normally applied directly to machinery but may be invoked where ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061 do not adequately cover a function (pqac-00000074).

A critical point: PL and SIL are assigned **per safety function**, not to the laboratory as a whole. A PL e-rated safety relay cannot retroactively make an uncertified robot reaction path PL e; the entire chain from sensor through logic to final element must satisfy the claimed integrity (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

The following table summarizes which standards bind a US university laboratory:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 1.2 The US Regulatory and Institutional Reality

In the United States, the ISO standards are voluntary consensus standards. They become effectively binding through several mechanisms: (a) OSHA's General Duty Clause (OSH Act §5(a)(1)) requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized serious hazards, and consensus standards serve as evidence of recognized practice; (b) **ANSI/RIA R15.06** is the US national robot safety consensus standard, historically harmonized with ISO 10218 (pqac-00000070); (c) university EHS committees and institutional review processes typically require documented risk assessments and may impose specific standards as conditions of approval; and (d) insurers may require compliance with specific standards as conditions of coverage.

**What published SDLs have actually done:** No published self-driving laboratory located in this review has documented formal third-party ISO 10218 certification or a completed ISO 13849-1 PL validation for its robot safety functions (pqac-00000072, pqac-00000073). The most comprehensive published safety architecture is **Safe-SDL**, which proposes a defense-in-depth framework with Operational Design Domains (ODDs), Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), and a CRUTD transactional safety protocol, but explicitly frames these as architectural proposals rather than certified implementations (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). This is a significant gap in the field: the SDL community has published extensively on workflow orchestration and optimization but very little on formal safety engineering.

### 1.3 Risk Assessment Methodology

For an SDL that combines software-controlled robots, furnaces, reactive powders, and remote supervision, **STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis)** is the most appropriate primary hazard analysis method. STPA models the system as a hierarchical control structure and examines unsafe control actions (UCAs) and causal scenarios across controllers, software, humans, and the environment (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Unlike FMEA, which focuses on individual component failures, STPA can address system-level interactions, feedback loops, software errors, and hazards that arise without any component failing—precisely the kind of scenario where an autonomous retry loop or a stale MQTT message causes harm (pqac-00000016). HAZOP is valuable for the furnace and powder-handling process nodes but requires adaptation for software-intensive systems (pqac-00000016). The recommended approach is: **ISO 12100** as the overall risk assessment framework, supplemented by **STPA** for the control structure, **HAZOP** for the furnace/powder process, and **FMEA/FMECA** for hardware component faults.

## 2. Specific Hazards, Quantified

### 2.1 Reactive Metal Powders

The dust explosion parameters for the powders in this system are summarized below:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For 10 μm aluminium powder, the maximum explosion pressure was 0.64 MPa and the deflagration index (Kst) was approximately 144 bar·m/s, measured at 200 g/m³ in a 20 L sphere (pqac-00000012). For 20 μm aluminium, Kst dropped to approximately 43 bar·m/s (pqac-00000012). Silicon dust has a reported Kst of approximately 120 bar·m/s at optimum concentration (pqac-00000013). These values are strongly particle-size dependent and must be obtained through lot-specific testing rather than handbook lookup (pqac-00000013). AlSi10Mg alloy-specific data were not found in the reviewed literature and must be tested independently.

**Static from a printed enclosure or plastic funnel is a real ignition source.** The MIE of fine aluminium powder is typically in the range of 10–50 mJ (extrapolation flagged—obtain lot-specific data), which is well within the energy range of electrostatic discharges from insulating plastic surfaces. FDM-printed enclosures (PLA, PETG, ABS) are insulators that can accumulate static charge during powder transfer. A powder-contact funnel or chute printed on a Bambu Lab printer would be an ungrounded insulating surface capable of generating brush discharges with energy sufficient to ignite fine aluminium dust. All conductive powder-handling equipment must be bonded and grounded with verified continuity. Non-conductive components must be replaced with static-dissipative or conductive alternatives, or eliminated from the powder-contact path.

**Enclosure and exhaust design:** The fume hood provides containment and local exhaust ventilation, but the exhaust system must be designed for combustible metal dust. Aluminium dust must not be routed into a general-purpose dust collector or a wet scrubber where water contact with fine aluminium could generate hydrogen. A dedicated, NFPA 484/660-compliant collection system with spark-resistant ductwork and appropriate isolation is required where adopted codes apply.

**Class D fire suppression:** Burning aluminium reacts violently with water (steam explosion risk and hydrogen generation) and with CO₂ (aluminium reduces CO₂ to carbon and aluminium oxide, sustaining combustion). Standard ABC extinguishers, water sprinklers, and CO₂ systems are all contraindicated. A Class D extinguishing agent (e.g., Met-L-X, sodium chloride-based, or dry sand) must be provided, and all on-site personnel must be trained to recognize that applying water to a metal fire will make it catastrophically worse.

### 2.2 Furnace Hazards

The critical furnace scenario is: the arm faults mid-insert with the furnace door open. If the safety system unconditionally removes arm power, the arm may drop a hot crucible, creating a spill of hot material and potentially a powder ignition event. The safe-state design must account for this: a mid-insert fault should trigger a controlled arm retraction or a hold-in-place before power removal, with the furnace door closing only after the arm is confirmed clear of the aperture. This requires a cause-and-effect matrix that addresses the arm, furnace, and their interaction states. Safe-SDL identifies thermal runaway and exothermic reactions as domain-specific hazards requiring real-time monitoring, forward prediction against a safe set, and automated shutdown (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008).

### 2.3 The Arm Itself

The AgileX PiPER is a 6-DOF arm with 1.5 kg payload and 626 mm reach, costing approximately $3k. At this price point, it almost certainly does not have certified safety-rated monitored stop, certified safe torque off, or validated stopping-time characterization with a published PFHD. This means the arm **cannot independently claim any Performance Level under ISO 13849-1** for its stopping behavior (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). An external safety relay, hardwired e-stop chain, and guard interlocking are not merely advisable—they are the only mechanism by which a defensible safety function can be constructed. The e-stop chain must use positive-opening contacts, dual-channel monitoring, manual reset with restart inhibit, and must not pass through MQTT, Tailscale, a Raspberry Pi, or any ordinary computing element.

At 1.5 kg payload and modest speed, the pinch and crush hazard is moderate but not negligible. A 1.5 kg payload at 1 m/s generates approximately 0.75 J of kinetic energy; the hazard is dominated by trapping geometry (e.g., crushing a finger between a crucible and a fixture) rather than free-space impact. The polycarbonate enclosure with interlocked access door is the primary mitigation for unexpected entry.

## 3. Fault Detection, Containment, and Safe-State Design

### 3.1 Spacecraft FDIR as the Transferable Model

The spacecraft Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) architecture provides the most directly transferable guard architecture for an SDL. In the Masat-1 CubeSat, FDIR is organized hierarchically: housekeeping collectors and safety functions detect component-level problems; a safety monitor correlates events with actions; and the flight planner makes the highest-level FDIR decisions (pqac-00000035). Recovery is attempted through command retries, parameter defaulting, watchdog-triggered resets, and receiver reinitialization. External EPS watchdogs periodically ping the onboard computer; after five failed pings they reset it. For unresolvable faults, the system transitions to a fail-safe mode: non-vital units are powered down and the spacecraft adopts a thermally and energetically safe configuration until ground contact (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038).

For an SDL, this translates to:
- **Level 0 (device):** Current/torque limits, encoder watchdogs, temperature monitors on each device.
- **Level 1 (subsystem):** Workspace envelope violation, balance disagreement, camera loss, stale heartbeat → local stop and retry (bounded).
- **Level 2 (orchestrator):** Mass-balance audit failure, protocol-sequence violation, consumed/remaining inventory mismatch → HOLD state and alert.
- **Level 3 (supervisor):** Escalation to human, system-wide safe state, furnace shutdown, ventilation assurance.

### 3.2 VLM Supervision: Useful but Not Safety-Critical

The LabRobFail benchmark evaluated vision-language models for robotic failure detection in chemical SDLs. The specialized LabRobFail-VLM achieves 90.83% failure-detection accuracy on seen environments, 77.21% temporal localization, and 83.18% severity assessment (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030). However, under distribution shift (unseen objects and scenes), detection accuracy drops to 71.02%, and temporal localization falls to 41.41% (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). These results are explicitly insufficient for safety-critical gating: a 29% miss rate on unseen conditions is far below the >99% reliability needed for a safety interlock (pqac-00000031). A VLM supervisor is appropriately used as a **supplementary anomaly-detection channel** that can trigger a HOLD state and page a human, but it must not be the sole gate on a hazardous action.

### 3.3 Safe-SDL's CRUTD Protocol

Safe-SDL proposes a transactional safety protocol: Create a request → Read/lock resources and capture state → simulate the transition → Test constraints → execute under monitoring → confirm the achieved state → abort/rollback on failure (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000061). This directly addresses the Q1 provenance failure where insert time was conflated with measurement time: the protocol separates requested, validated, executed, and confirmed states with distinct timestamps.

### 3.4 Recovery vs. Halt: The Autonomous Retry Problem

The critical design question is: when should the system retry, and when should it halt and page a human? The spacecraft pattern is clear: bounded local recovery at the lowest level, with escalation on failure (pqac-00000037). The SDL equivalent is:
- **Retry:** A balance reading that disagrees by <1% on first attempt → re-weigh once. A gripper position error within repeatability → re-approach once.
- **Halt:** A balance disagreement >5%, a dropped object, a current spike, an unrecognized object in the workspace, any thermal anomaly, any loss of communication with safety-critical devices, or **any second consecutive failure of the same type**.

The autonomous retry loop that converts a recoverable fault into a catastrophic one is the most dangerous failure mode. The design rule is: **finite retry budget (typically 1–2), monotonically decreasing scope with each retry, automatic escalation to HOLD after budget exhaustion, and human-cleared recovery from HOLD** (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000036).

## 3b. Remote Supervision

### Latency, Bandwidth, and Video Quality

Remote vehicle operation studies indicate that communication latency above approximately 50 ms makes displayed imagery outdated for useful interaction; 5G networks may reduce latency below 10 ms (pqac-00000022). Streaming video from four HD cameras requires at least 50 Mbit/s (pqac-00000022). A latency spike of 3–4 seconds caused a remote operator to miss that a vehicle was approaching warehouse racks, creating crash risk (pqac-00000021). For an SDL, this means the Tailscale VPN must provide consistent sub-100 ms round-trip latency, and the system must automatically transition to HOLD if video latency exceeds a defined threshold.

### The Out-of-the-Loop Problem

When a remote human is only summoned on exception, recovery time depends critically on the specificity of the alert. A specified failure (e.g., "balance timeout on station 3") took approximately 29 seconds to understand, whereas an unspecified problem took approximately 162 seconds (pqac-00000022). This is a factor of 5.6×, which has direct implications for alarm design: every alert must include the failure type, affected station, current system state, available actions, and recommended response. HMD-360 presentation produced faster decisions than screen-based viewing—approximately 80% of screen-based decision time and more than twice as many correct responses (pqac-00000025).

### Remote E-Stop Design

When the responsible human is 1,000 km away and the only people in the room are undergraduates who did not start the experiment, the e-stop system must satisfy two independent requirements: (a) a **physical e-stop button** accessible to anyone in the room, clearly labeled, requiring no knowledge of the experiment, connected to the hardwired safety chain, and (b) a **remote stop command** that is software-initiated but terminates in a hardwired safety relay or contactor, not merely an MQTT message. The remote stop must be tested end-to-end, and the system must enter a safe state automatically on loss of the remote supervision link (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). Maritime autonomous system requirements specify that communication links must be treated as safety-control channels, with link quality monitored and tied to operational-state thresholds (pqac-00000024).

## 4. The Control Plane

### 4.1 Critical Evaluation of EOS vs. Existing Infrastructure

The group's existing stack is **MQTT (HiveMQ) + MongoDB Atlas + Hugging Face Spaces + GitHub Actions**, with Tailscale networking and an Opentrons HTTP API. Q3 recommended EOS. The migration cost of adopting EOS or any monolithic SDL orchestrator would be substantial: it would require replacing or wrapping the existing MQTT device bus, re-implementing the Opentrons integration, migrating the MongoDB data model, and retraining students on a new framework—all for uncertain gain given the group's already-functioning device communication layer.

**The defensible architecture keeps MQTT as the device bus and adds an orchestrator above it.** This is precisely the pattern used by OCTOPUS, which implements a hierarchical client/interface-node/master-node/module-node architecture with TCP/IP-based process modularization, supporting concurrent multi-user jobs from heterogeneous devices (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000067). OCTOPUS's user-optimal scheduler reduced example total job times from 10 to 5.5–6.5 hours compared to first-come-first-served serialization (pqac-00000062).

**What MQTT alone lacks and what must be added above it:**
- **Multi-user queuing and fair scheduling:** MQTT is a pub/sub bus, not a scheduler. An orchestrator must maintain job queues, unique job IDs, resource locks, and a scheduling policy (pqac-00000067).
- **Authentication and authorization:** HiveMQ supports ACLs, but experiment-level authorization (who may run what protocol with what materials) requires an application-layer gate.
- **Crash recovery and idempotency:** MQTT QoS 2 provides at-most-once or exactly-once message delivery, but protocol-level crash recovery requires durable state: each command must have an idempotency key, and the orchestrator must be able to resume from a known good state after restart.
- **Observability:** MongoDB provides storage but not real-time dashboards. Add structured event streams with timestamps, state assertions, and health metrics.

### 4.2 Data Provenance and Persistent Identifiers

**RO-Crate** packages research objects—data, workflows, software, metadata, and provenance—into self-describing JSON-LD containers using Schema.org vocabulary (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000060). **PROV-O** provides the W3C ontology for representing provenance: entities, activities, and agents with generation, usage, derivation, and attribution relationships (pqac-00000055). Together, they can package an SDL campaign: the requested protocol, the authorized execution plan, the sensor-observed physical events, the resulting data, and the complete chain of custody.

The Q1 failure—conflating insert time with measurement time—is precisely the provenance failure that RO-Crate + PROV-O is designed to prevent. A prospective instrument trace should record each experimental event with its control source (human, script, optimizer, agent), distinguishing the requested action from the executed action from the observed outcome (pqac-00000059). The CRUTD protocol from Safe-SDL provides the operational model: the requested command, the pre-operation state snapshot, the simulation/validation result, the execution event, the post-execution sensor confirmation, and any abort/rollback events should all be recorded as distinct provenance entities with separate timestamps (pqac-00000061).

For DOI minting: package completed campaigns as Workflow-Run RO-Crates, deposit to Zenodo, and mint DOIs. This provides immutable, citable records of what physically happened.

## 5. Human Factors and the Undergraduate Reality

### 5.1 Training and Error Rates

The SDL literature is qualitatively consistent: human technicians remain essential for loading plates, opening packages, replacing consumables, replenishing reagents, removing waste, calibrating equipment, and resolving faults (pqac-00000043). Laboratory automation is generally fixed and highly structured, requiring carefully specified layouts; even small equipment or consumable changes can require substantial reprogramming (pqac-00000043). Virtual reality training has been shown to reduce operator errors, but may increase stress for complex tasks due to the greater information load (from the Brunzini et al. 2024 training methodology study).

### 5.2 Human Time Costs in SDLs

No published SDL located in this review provides quantitative utilization rates (percentage of wall-clock time spent running vs. idle) or calibrated human-time savings. The qualitative evidence is consistent: autonomous Bayesian optimization campaigns have reached optima in under 30 hours, and batched reaction optimization achieved 192 reactions in four days—approximately 4× the throughput of sequential human operation (pqac-00000046). However, these throughput gains are interleaved with human effort for electrode cleaning, vial loading, chemical preparation, purification troubleshooting, and consumable replacement (pqac-00000045). Dispensing solids below approximately 20 mg and handling heterogeneous mixtures remain difficult to automate (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048).

### 5.3 Design Choices That Improve Utilization

The most impactful design choices are: (a) **magazine/rack capacity** sized so that consumable exhaustion does not interrupt overnight runs; (b) **scheduled human touchpoints** (e.g., daily morning restocking) rather than on-demand interruptions; (c) **batching** to consolidate related experiments into continuous runs; (d) **finite consumable accounting** so the system knows when to stop before running out; and (e) **progressive autonomy** starting with the simplest, most constrained operations and expanding only after demonstrated reliability (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

**Flagged extrapolation:** The precise throughput fraction lost to restocking and low-utilization windows is not well-characterized in the published literature. This is an open measurement gap that this group could contribute to by instrumenting their own system.

## 6. The First 90 Days

The following phased timeline places risk assessment and physical safeguards before software commissioning and narrowly bounded unattended trials:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### Key Constraints

**The first experiment that can honestly run without a person in the room** is an inert-powder (alumina) dispensing-and-weighing loop, with no furnace, no reactive metals, restricted room access, remote monitoring, hardwired safeguards, finite consumable budget, and automatic halt on anomaly. This is achievable within 90 days if the safety infrastructure is in place.

**Reactive metal powder handling unattended is not a defensible 90-day milestone.** It requires lot-specific explosibility testing, validated dust-handling controls, approved exhaust/collection design, demonstrated static-control measures, incident-free attended and remotely supervised operating hours, and institutional/fire-authority approval. Treating a fume hood, a printed enclosure, a camera feed, or a remote operator as explosion protection is not defensible.

### Minimum Documentation Package for EHS Review

The minimum defensible package includes: (1) scope and system description; (2) ISO 12100 risk assessment register; (3) STPA control structure analysis; (4) dust hazard analysis per NFPA 484/660; (5) SDS inventory and quantity limits; (6) cell layout with safety distances; (7) safety circuit schematics with component ratings; (8) ventilation basis of design; (9) fire-response plan with Class D agent selection; (10) SOPs for attended and unattended operation; (11) training plan and competency records; (12) commissioning and validation protocol; (13) remote-supervision concept of operations; and (14) management-of-change procedure.

### What Is Legally Required vs. Best Practice vs. Prudent

- **Legally required** (where applicable): Risk assessment documenting recognized hazards and feasible controls (OSHA General Duty Clause); machine guarding (29 CFR 1910.212); combustible-metal fire prevention per adopted fire code; emergency-stop accessible to room occupants; training for all personnel.
- **Best practice:** ISO 12100 risk assessment framework; STPA for the control structure; ISO 13849-1 PL derivation for safety functions; Safe-SDL CRUTD protocol; RO-Crate provenance; progressive autonomy with regression after incidents.
- **Prudent but optional:** VLM anomaly detection as supplementary channel; immersive (HMD-360) remote supervision interface; formal verification of safety-kernel software; digital-twin pre-validation of each experiment.

### What Is Unknown

Several questions remain genuinely open: (1) no published SDL has reported a formal safety-validation protocol or third-party certification for its robot safety functions; (2) no quantitative SDL utilization data exist in the reviewed literature; (3) the AgileX PiPER's stopping-time characterization, PFHD, and diagnostic coverage are not publicly documented; (4) AlSi10Mg alloy-specific dust explosion parameters are not available in the reviewed literature; and (5) the long-term reliability of VLM-based anomaly detection under distribution shift in production SDL environments is an open research question (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032)."}
